# DPO Loss (Rafailov et al., 2023)

In *"Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model"*, the objective is:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}(\pi_\theta; \pi_{\text{ref}}) = -\,\mathbb{E}_{(x,\,y_w,\,y_l)\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\log \sigma\!\left(\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w \mid x)} \;-\; \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l \mid x)}\right)\right]
$$

where:
- $x$ is the prompt, $y_w$ is the preferred completion and $y_l$ is the dispreferred one.
- $\pi_\theta$ is the policy being trained, and $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ is the frozen reference model (typically the SFT model).
- $\sigma$ is the logistic sigmoid.
- $\beta$ is the KL-penalty strength.

## What plays the role of the reward

The scaled log-ratio between the policy and the reference model acts as the reward:

$$
\hat{r}_\theta(x, y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)}
$$

This is why the paper says the language model is "secretly a reward model."

**Where it comes from.** The KL-constrained RLHF objective has a closed-form optimal policy:

$$
\pi^*(y \mid x) = \frac{1}{Z(x)}\, \pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)\, \exp\!\left(\tfrac{1}{\beta} r(x,y)\right)
$$

Solving this for the reward gives:

$$
r(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi^*(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)} + \beta \log Z(x)
$$

You then substitute this into the Bradley–Terry preference model, $p(y_w \succ y_l \mid x) = \sigma\big(r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l)\big)$. The intractable partition function $Z(x)$ depends only on $x$, so it cancels in the difference. That cancellation is what leaves the loss above.

**Interpretation of the gradient.** The paper shows that each example's gradient is weighted by $\sigma\big(\hat{r}_\theta(x,y_l) - \hat{r}_\theta(x,y_w)\big)$. This weight is large when the implicit reward wrongly ranks the dispreferred completion higher. The update raises the likelihood of $y_w$ and lowers that of $y_l$.

Because $Z(x)$ was dropped, the implicit reward is only defined up to a function of the prompt. It is meaningful for comparing completions of the same prompt, not as an absolute score across prompts.
